events.title: Bartram’s Garden Photo Exhibit at Studio 34
events.venue: Studio 34, 4522 Baltimore Avenue, Philadelphia, PA 19143
events.description: Bartram’s Garden is the oldest surviving botanical garden in North America. Located in an urban neighborhood, it is a gem of nature that may seem incongruous to first-time visitors. In the 1720s, botanist John Bartram built a stone house overlooking the Schuylkill River, and began farming the 107 acres of land around it. In his spare time, Bartram followed his interest in native plant species and traveled widely collecting plants and seeds from th northern shores of Nova Scotia to the southern tip of Florida. He founded a botanical garden on the five acre plot between his house and the river and developed a nursery that sold native plants and served as a base for correspondence with other botanists on both sides of the Atlantic. Welcome to Chekhov’s Banana Peel, the debut production from 21st Century Commedia. This high-octane, relentlessly physical production takes the complete works of Anton Chekhov, the undisputed master of existential subtext and melancholy drama and strips away the subtext entirely. Armed with nothing but physical theatre, high-energy clowning, precision mime, and a healthy dose of theatrical anarchy, our ensemble attempts the impossible: a breakneck, abridged marathon of Chekhov's greatest plays.

events.description:
Paul Ramírez Jonas’ monumental artwork plays the song “My Country ‘Tis of Thee” in its entirety—all but the final note. Participants must pull a lever to ring the last note on a 600-pound bell at the base of the sculpture to complete the song, a metaphor for how we can work together as a society to fulfill the unfinished promises of our nation’s founding. events.title: Flood Stones Rising
events.venue: Art Room Studio
events.description:
"Flood Stones Rising" explores time, location and memory. Grounded in deep listening improvisation, we activate personal story, vocalization practice and physical gesture. Small stones anchor the space and our bodies exploring sonic, physical and metaphorical resonances. Building on and expanding our ‘carry with me this place’ practice, “Flood Stones Rising” embraces the flooding of memory and tension between erasure and memory in ourselves and the landscape.
This quote from Toni Morrison inspires our process:
"Floods" is the word they use, but in fact it is not flooding; it is remembering. Remembering where it used to be. All water has a perfect memory and is forever trying to get back to where it was.

events.description: Bartram’s Garden is the oldest surviving botanical garden in North America. Located in an urban neighborhood, it is a gem of nature that may seem incongruous to first-time visitors. In the 1720s, botanist John Bartram built a stone house overlooking the Schuylkill River, and began farming the 107 acres of land around it. In his spare time, Bartram followed his interest in native plant species and traveled widely collecting plants and seeds from th northern shores of Nova Scotia to the southern tip of Florida. He founded a botanical garden on the five acre plot between his house and the river and developed a nursery that sold native plants and served as a base for correspondence with other botanists on both sides of the Atlantic. events.venue: Asian Arts Initiative Black Box Theater
events.description:
Turkish-Colombian-American performer, Izzy Sazak, takes the audience on a wild ride; unpacking the awkward beauty of growing up mixed, caught between two empires worth of daddy issues and messy history. Tuzluk lovingly deconstructs the myth of the neo-liberal hero-man; mixing geopolitics with a hilarious, heartfelt and fast paced examination of identity and inheritance. * Tuzluk: turkish for “salt shaker”, and the colloquial name for the popular children’s paper fortune teller game.

events.title: Flood Stones Rising
events.venue: Art Room Studio
events.description:
"Flood Stones Rising" explores time, location and memory. Grounded in deep listening improvisation, we activate personal story, vocalization practice and physical gesture. Small stones anchor the space and our bodies exploring sonic, physical and metaphorical resonances. Building on and expanding our ‘carry with me this place’ practice, “Flood Stones Rising” embraces the flooding of memory and tension between erasure and memory in ourselves and the landscape.
This quote from Toni Morrison inspires our process:
"Floods" is the word they use, but in fact it is not flooding; it is remembering. Remembering where it used to be. All water has a perfect memory and is forever trying to get back to where it was.

events.description:
A year after her mother’s death, a poet in recovery moves home to Philadelphia to get a divorce and start a new life. events.description: Bartram’s Garden is the oldest surviving botanical garden in North America. Located in an urban neighborhood, it is a gem of nature that may seem incongruous to first-time visitors. In the 1720s, botanist John Bartram built a stone house overlooking the Schuylkill River, and began farming the 107 acres of land around it. In his spare time, Bartram followed his interest in native plant species and traveled widely collecting plants and seeds from th northern shores of Nova Scotia to the southern tip of Florida. He founded a botanical garden on the five acre plot between his house and the river and developed a nursery that sold native plants and served as a base for correspondence with other botanists on both sides of the Atlantic. Inspired by Aeschylus' "The Suppliants" - one of the oldest surviving plays in the Western canon - this new ensemble-driven performance reimagines an ancient story through the lens of Appalachian folklore.
What begins as a tale from the distant past slowly unfolds into something far more immediate: a meditation on refuge, belonging, and the choices communities make when confronted with outsiders seeking safety.
Blending elements of Greek tragedy, folk traditions, movement, and devised performance, the work explores how stories travel across generations and why certain myths refuse to disappear.

events.venue: Cherry Street Pier, 121 N Christopher Columbus Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19106
events.description:
Paul Ramírez Jonas’ monumental artwork plays the song “My Country ‘Tis of Thee” in its entirety—all but the final note. Participants must pull a lever to ring the last note on a 600-pound bell at the base of the sculpture to complete the song, a metaphor for how we can work together as a society to fulfill the unfinished promises of our nation’s founding. events.title: soft spot
events.venue: Icebox Project Space Gallery
events.description: "soft spot" is a dance work for the child within us, uninhibited and open to the potential of everything. Vyette Tiya and her collaborators use the language of movement to explore tenderness, vulnerability, and intimacy — a glance that turns into a grasp, a tease that turns into a collision, a game that tumbles into freefall. Framed through a series of vignettes, "soft spot" asks: how do we wish to be seen? Who can see us? How do we remain tender in a world that hardens us?

events.description:
An original solo show about a very unoriginal topic: Dating.
In the absence of a romantic relationship, the next best thing is the attention of a rapt audience. For as long as Tess has been single (forever), the best part of dates has been telling stories about them after. Now she’s ready to share them with everyone else [with names redacted]. Over this 75-minute show, Tess weaves personal storytelling and audience participation about what it means to be 35, ready to mingle, and obsessed with finding meaning in everything. Part comedy show, part singles event (for Tess), all catharsis. Bring your single straight male friends. Seriously.
*Not actually a work in progress show; the single woman IS the work in progress, y'know?

events.title: Flood Stones Rising
events.venue: Art Room Studio
events.description:
"Flood Stones Rising" explores time, location and memory. Grounded in deep listening improvisation, we activate personal story, vocalization practice and physical gesture. Small stones anchor the space and our bodies exploring sonic, physical and metaphorical resonances. Building on and expanding our ‘carry with me this place’ practice, “Flood Stones Rising” embraces the flooding of memory and tension between erasure and memory in ourselves and the landscape.
This quote from Toni Morrison inspires our process:
"Floods" is the word they use, but in fact it is not flooding; it is remembering. Remembering where it used to be. All water has a perfect memory and is forever trying to get back to where it was.

Welcome to the Bearded Ladies’ Hairport, an interactive installation & performance series built on 16-years of accumulated baggage from a queer cabaret company devoted to art, care, mess, and community. While you’re waiting for a flight that may never take off, unpack your baggage and rifle through some of ours. events.venue: Studio 34, 4522 Baltimore Avenue, Philadelphia, PA 19143
events.description: Bartram’s Garden is the oldest surviving botanical garden in North America. Located in an urban neighborhood, it is a gem of nature that may seem incongruous to first-time visitors. In the 1720s, botanist John Bartram built a stone house overlooking the Schuylkill River, and began farming the 107 acres of land around it. In his spare time, Bartram followed his interest in native plant species and traveled widely collecting plants and seeds from th northern shores of Nova Scotia to the southern tip of Florida. He founded a botanical garden on the five acre plot between his house and the river and developed a nursery that sold native plants and served as a base for correspondence with other botanists on both sides of the Atlantic. events.venue: Cherry Street Pier, 121 N Christopher Columbus Blvd, Philadelphia, PA 19106
events.description:
Paul Ramírez Jonas’ monumental artwork plays the song “My Country ‘Tis of Thee” in its entirety—all but the final note. Participants must pull a lever to ring the last note on a 600-pound bell at the base of the sculpture to complete the song, a metaphor for how we can work together as a society to fulfill the unfinished promises of our nation’s founding. This artwork promotes civic engagement by providing a public site to speak, listen, and learn from one another, and to bring people together to imagine a more inclusive future that embraces the complexities of our past.

events.title: Echoes of Dammām
events.venue: Icebox Project Space Gallery
events.description:
Echoes of Dammām is a multimedia storytelling performance that follows fragmented stories gathered around dammām, a ritual drumming practice from Bushehr, a port city in southern Iran.
On stage, live narration moves alongside projected video, field recordings, and layered sound. Drums, voices, images, silence, and memory appear in fragments, tracing how grief, resistance, and the struggle for freedom can live inside sonic and bodily practices. Drawing from ethnographic fieldwork in Bushehr, the performance does not tell a single linear story. Instead, it creates an intimate audiovisual space where ritual mourning, Black musical heritage, histories of circulation and loss, and personal memory echo through one another.

events.description: Fuck it, I love You is an extension of my work with vignettes, duration and repetition. events.title: Utopian Hotline. A Telephone Hotline, A Vinyl Record, A Performance
events.venue: Franklin Institute Fels Planetarium
events.description:
Co-Presented with The Franklin Institute
Is anyone out there? Is anyone listening? Are we alone? In 1977, NASA launched the twin Voyager spacecrafts to try and answer these questions. Aboard both is the Golden Record, an artifact intended to communicate who and what we are. events.description:
When we shut out seeing and hearing, what does the body begin to sense, feel and express?
Soseul Dawon, meaning solitude in a quiet garden in Korean, is a movement laboratory that interrogates the paradox of sensory deprivation. Does it compensate through heightened senses elsewhere? Is somatic sensitivity amplified as a result of quieting distractions channeled through eyes and ears? events.description: “400 Miles from Regular" is a one-person show about a woman in mid-life who has decided it’s now or never to become who she truly is. Can she finally summon the courage to stand up to her controlling soon to be ex-husband, her toxically positive sister, and her video-game addicted teenage son. Can she surprise herself and walk away to an uncertain future? "400 Miles from Regular" is the galvanizing story of a woman who steps into the unknown, not out of despair, but out of an exhilarating will to grow and build a better future.

events.title: Echoes of Dammām
events.venue: Icebox Project Space Gallery
events.description:
Echoes of Dammām is a multimedia storytelling performance that follows fragmented stories gathered around dammām, a ritual drumming practice from Bushehr, a port city in southern Iran.
On stage, live narration moves alongside projected video, field recordings, and layered sound. Drums, voices, images, silence, and memory appear in fragments, tracing how grief, resistance, and the struggle for freedom can live inside sonic and bodily practices. Drawing from ethnographic fieldwork in Bushehr, the performance does not tell a single linear story. Instead, it creates an intimate audiovisual space where ritual mourning, Black musical heritage, histories of circulation and loss, and personal memory echo through one another.

Told through queer, feminist, and postcolonial lenses, it probes the tangled dynamics of power, desire, and identity. The actors playing Laura and Carmilla alternate roles each performance, highlighting the question: who is the predator, and who is the prey?

events.title: Residue Solo
events.venue: Icebox Project Space Gallery
events.description: Residue Solo is a durational performance built around a single, distilled movement. As the final work in a three-part series, it carries forward the larger project’s gradual reduction of form, arriving at an action that is repeated, sustained, and allowed to change through time. The performance attends to endurance, repetition, and the subtle shifts that emerge when there is nowhere else to go. Notice Me, Gwyneth is a solo show that explores Matthew's attempt to impress his aloof yet loving boss, navigate what the future holds for the doting boyfriend who he's uncertain about, and always come out looking better than his workplace frenemy. events.description:
How can we communicate when words fail? If the need is desperate enough, can we escape language and still be understood?

How do we feel about what we have created together?
What might we learn about our inner world, how we connect to others, and the larger implications of what we see in our temporary social field?

events.venue: Franklin Institute Planetarium
events.description:
Is anyone out there? Is anyone listening? Are we alone? In 1977, NASA launched the twin Voyager spacecrafts to try and answer these questions. Aboard both is the Golden Record, an artifact intended to communicate who and what we are. After almost 50 years and over 13 billion miles, this proverbial message in a bottle is the farthest human-made object from earth. If we were to send another message into the distant future, what message would we send?
To answer this, Mitu created a public telephone hotline (646-694-8050) prompting people to leave messages to the future. Utopian Hotline uses these voicemails alongside interviews with NASA astronauts, astrophysicists, astronomers, and middle school students to create a moment of community. This p

Created by Continuum Dance Project, with projection by Ernesto Galan, the piece blends powerful, expressive choreography with themes of attention, care, and reciprocity; inviting viewers to feel, not just observe, our place within nature’s cycles.
Inspired by Robin Wall Kimmerer’s 'Braiding Sweetgrass' and a personal sense of disconnection, the work challenges audiences to reconsider their relationship to the seasons, and the land we inhabit. Designed for both indoor and outdoor stages, Echoes of Renewal is adaptable, evocative, and timely; an experience that resonates long after the final movement.

events.venue: Asian Arts Initiative Third Floor
events.description:
Echoes of Tranquility is an interdisciplinary performance experience combining contemporary dance, live piano, and a lecture on Japanese philosophy and aesthetics. Created by choreographer Yuki Ishiguro in collaboration with pianist Yuko Gordon, the work explores concepts such as Ma (space and interval), Yūgen (subtle mystery), and ritual embodiment through movement, music, light, and silence.
Inspired by the historical exchange between Eastern and Western art, the performance blends contemporary dance with Japanese aesthetics to create a poetic and meditative theatrical experience. Audiences are invited not only to watch the performance, but also to engage with the philosophical ideas that shaped its creation.

events.title: Tstmrkt
events.venue: Circus Campus
events.description:
TSTMRKT (pronounced “Test Market”) is a performance art sketch comedy amalgamation held together with film loops, cut-n-paste theatre, and a relentless soundtrack. There is no “sound person” running the effects. It’s just a “start” button and a bag of nerves.
Once the actor hits “start” on the playback, the film collages and sound effects are triggered only by time. It’s the actor’s task to keep track of each second that passes, each syllable that is uttered, and each movement created in space. If anything is off, the entire thing falls apart. It’s a theatrical tightrope. You’ve never seen anything like it.

The Voynich Manuscript is a real, 15th century codex written in an unknown language. Alongside 240 pages of text in a unique alphabet, it depicts people bathing in strange contraptions, botanical details of unknown plants, and astrological star charts unlike any on earth. Some scholars suggest it is a complex hoax, yet text analysis and information theory suggest the letter and word frequency match those of a real language.

Philadelphia performance artist Thomas Choinacky humorously assembles ordinary objects and their curious histories. Sitting around a tabletop, a small audience of ten gets an up-close view of the action.
